bull.t: Diversified recurring revenue and hospital robotics
bull.b: Recurring software, advertising and hospital contracts can reduce reliance on per-delivery volume. Hospital robotics adds a potentially higher-margin, multi-year revenue stream and broadens Serve’s exposure beyond consumer food delivery.

bull.t: Expanding fleet, partnerships and market footprint
bull.b: A larger deployed fleet and broader geographic presence can improve utilization, operating leverage and partner appeal. Continued DoorDash growth and new marketplace launches provide structural avenues to replace weaker Uber volumes.

bull.t: Strong liquidity and low balance-sheet leverage
bull.b: Substantial liquidity and minimal leverage give Serve time to fund autonomy, fleet and market investments while restructuring its channel mix. The repaired capitalization lowers immediate solvency pressure compared with its earlier negative-equity periods.

bear.t: Severe losses and sustained cash burn
bear.b: Cash consumption remains disproportionate to revenue, while deeply negative gross margins show that current delivery economics are not yet self-funding. Unless scale materially improves unit costs, Serve may require continued financing despite its cash reserves.

bear.t: Uber partnership reversal and reduced revenue outlook
bear.b: The loss of expected Uber volume exposes concentration and partner-dependence risk, while the guidance cut lowers the near-term commercialization base. Replacing that demand through other channels may take time and could delay operating leverage.

bear.t: Integration barriers constrain addressable delivery demand
bear.b: Limited merchant and platform integration restricts the orders Serve can efficiently access, regardless of its available robot capacity. Products such as Beacon may expand demand, but adoption and deployment requirements create a persistent scaling constraint.
